verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains the verse as saying that God revealed the Book to the Prophet in order that he bring mankind from darkness into light. “Mankind” is unrestricted by the wording and therefore encompasses humanity, not merely the Prophet’s own community or its believers; Qur’anic addresses to all nations, the People of the Book, and the Prophet’s outreach beyond the Arabs support this universality. Yet the sūrah’s conclusion, describing the Qur’an as a proclamation for mankind so that they may be warned, indicates that those who truly emerge from darkness into light are believers.

The Prophet is described as bringing people forth because he is a manifest means of guidance, not its independent source. God alone ultimately guides, directly or through intermediaries. Thus the statement that the Prophet does not guide whom he wishes negates his primary and independent guidance, while the statement that he guides to a straight path affirms his mediated role. “By the command of their Lord” makes this dependence explicit.

Darkness (al-ẓulumāt) and light (al-nūr) respectively signify misguidance and guidance. Darkness is plural because misguidance follows diverse, mutually inconsistent desires; light is singular because guidance derives from the one truth, whose aspects are harmonious. The lam in li-tukhrij al-nās is a lam of purpose, not consequence: if it meant consequence, all people would necessarily become believers. Although divine grace is universal and its effect depends on people’s preparedness, the verse’s purpose is legislative: God commands, forbids, sends messengers, and reveals scriptures intending the human benefits that follow—faith, forgiveness, righteous action, purification from Satan’s harm, happiness, and Paradise. Divine speech and the messengers’ clarification establish decisive proof; purposes stated in commands are genuine purposes, just as drinking is the purpose of an order to bring water.

God’s actions and commands have wisdom and purposes, but He is wholly free of need. Their purposes concern the perfection and benefit of creation, not a perfection acquired by God. No benefit or harm moves, governs, or compels Him; He owns all things, is owned by none, decrees over all, and is decreed over by none. Intellect infers from particular divine acts that they rest on benefit and purpose, while recognizing that such benefit does not determine the divine Essence. Thus divine purposes differ from human purposes in two respects: God is not perfected by their ends, and neither benefit nor harm impels Him. Al-Mizan consequently rejects both sides of the Ashʿarite–Muʿtazilite dispute: God neither acts purposelessly by a merely decisive will nor acts because a benefit compels Him to act rather than refrain.

The shift to “by the permission of their Lord” foregrounds Lordship: the idolaters themselves are under the lordship of the God with whom they associate partners, and this prepares the sūrah’s argument for the Unity of Lordship. The path leads to God as al-ʿAzīz, whom nothing can subdue and who subdues everything; all true might belongs to Him, and others possess it only through Him and by His permission. He is also al-Ḥamīd: since every chosen beauty culminates in Him, all praise belongs to Him. The Book is therefore both light, distinguishing truth from falsehood, good from evil, and happiness from misery, and a clear path gathering its travelers and leading them to the Almighty, the Praiseworthy.

These two attributes introduce the sūrah’s central call: people must recognize God’s lordship and blessings, give thanks rather than deny Him, believe the messengers’ promise of Paradise and warning of wrath and punishment, fear His invincible might, and reflect on the signs of His Lordship. He is Praiseworthy in rewarding believers, punishing disbelievers, and bestowing innumerable blessings. Al-Mizan regards a report cited from Abū Hayyan, which makes might refer to God’s capacity to reveal a miraculous Book and praise to the blessing of guidance, as unrelated to this sūrah’s context, perhaps borrowed from a distinct Qur’anic context. It reports al-Rāzī’s explanation that al-ʿAzīz precedes al-Ḥamīd because knowledge of divine power precedes knowledge of His knowledge and self-sufficiency, but treats other claims—such as giving negative attributes precedence over affirmative ones, or making the two names chiefly an encouragement because travelers gain might and praise—as at most derived benefits rather than the principal explanation.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s ownership of everything in the heavens and earth is real and absolute. It establishes the meanings of His might and praiseworthiness: all power and domination proceed from Him, and every one of His acts is commendable because He acts in what is genuinely His. Criticism of an act arises where the agent lacks rightful ownership; this cannot apply to God. The threat of severe punishment for the faithless displays His might in subjugating those who reject His call and are ungrateful for His blessings.

Those who “prefer the life of this world to the Hereafter” actively choose its fleeting enjoyments over the abiding life to come. Preferring the Hereafter does not mean abandoning this world altogether, since earthly life is the necessary passage through which one prepares for the Hereafter. Rather, it means making the Hereafter the ultimate aim and employing worldly life as its means. Making this world the final aim entails forsaking the Hereafter; if the Hereafter were truly acknowledged, it would necessarily be the chief objective. Since human beings naturally seek a happy life, and life does not end at death, their earthly deeds determine their good or evil condition in the everlasting Hereafter.

Human choices between righteousness and transgression are a dīn, or way of life, and a sabīl, or path. God guides every species to its proper happiness and perfection; human perfection lies in communal life ordered by the divine standards that accord with the innate nature God created. This is God’s straight path. Whoever follows divine guidance and this sound disposition walks it, while whoever follows lower impulses, Satanic illusion, and disregard of divine guidance departs from it. Accordingly, the disbelievers’ attachment to this world amounts to renouncing the Hereafter, and hence to denying God’s Unity and prophethood.

Their barring others from God’s way and seeking to make it crooked means that they refuse God’s true religion, deter others from faith in God, the Hereafter, and His laws, and seek to introduce deviation into His path by establishing some alternative social direction. They attempt to find defects in the path so that people will abandon it, and for this they are in extreme error. Al-Mizan rejects readings that make their act merely perceiving crookedness in the path and then defaming it, or misleading its followers simply by discrediting it; such readings misconstrue the intended distortion of religion.

verses.4:
Al-Mizan holds that lisān means language, and that “his people” and “to them” refer in each case to the particular messenger’s people. Every messenger was sent speaking the language prevalent among the community with which he lived and communicated, so that he could make the divine message clear. The verse does not mean that “his people” refers only to Prophet Muḥammad, for that would require all revelation, including the Torah given to Mūsā, to have been conveyed in Arabic to the Arabs. Nor does it concern ancestral language as such: Lot’s mission to the Hebrew-speaking inhabitants of Muʾtafakāt, despite his migration from Syriac-speaking Chaldea, illustrates that a people are the community to whom the messenger is sent.

This linguistic principle does not confine the missions of the major prophets to one linguistic community. Abraham called the Arabs of Ḥijāz to Hajj, Mūsā called Pharaoh and his people, Muḥammad addressed the world and the Qur’an calls Jews, Christians, and others, while Noah’s mission was universal. The purpose of the verse is not that messengers receive miraculous linguistic ability or that they bear an impossible burden, but that they use the current language of their community to expound what revelation seeks from them. Beyond this clarification, neither messengers nor anyone else possesses guidance or misguidance; these belong to God alone.

God’s guidance and misguidance nevertheless operate according to a fixed and wise system: those who heed the truth are guided, while those who reject it and follow base desire undergo misguidance. This misguidance is metaphorical and is not to be understood as a punitive act initiated by God. The precedence of “Allah leads astray whomever He wishes” over “He guides whomsoever He wishes” serves the context of divine might. A person’s refusal of God’s call does not overpower Him, nor does anyone act within His dominion without His permission. The straying of the misguided, as much as the guidance of the guided, occurs by His decree and displays His might. Yet neither their misguidance harms Him nor their guidance benefits Him; as al-ʿAzīz and al-Ḥakīm, He acts neither arbitrarily nor without purpose, but through a sound and consistent order.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains that the mission of Mūsā is cited because this sūrah chiefly warns and reminds people of divine majesty, and Moses’s mission, accompanied by signs and manifest authority, is among the clearest prophetic displays of that majesty. His charge to bring his people from darkness into light parallels Muḥammad’s charge and expresses the common prophetic call to spiritual ascent and the enrichment of the soul. The verse is not principally an elaboration of the preceding statement that messengers are sent in their people’s language. Nor do the signs sent with Moses mean the Torah’s verses alone; they include his other miracles, such as the serpent and the radiant hand. The Qur’an says that the Torah was revealed to Moses, not that he was sent with it as the sign validating his prophethood.

Unlike the command to Muḥammad, Moses’s command does not explicitly say “by the command of their Lord,” because the imperative to bring forth his people itself implicitly contains divine permission. “The days of God” are particular days in which His decree, sovereignty, and Unity are conspicuously manifested or are destined to be manifested. They include death, which discloses the rule of the Hereafter; the Day of Resurrection, when every soul stands alone and all affairs belong to God; days of retribution such as the destruction of Noah’s, ʿĀd’s, and Thamūd’s peoples; and days of special blessing, such as Noah’s disembarkation from the ark and Abraham’s deliverance from the fire. Both blessings and punishments manifest divine will and majesty, so the expression cannot be restricted to either alone.

The signs in these days benefit every al-ṣabbār and al-shakūr: the former is intensely patient in adversity, and the latter profoundly grateful for blessings.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains that Moses reminds the Children of Israel of Allah’s favor in saving them from Pharaoh’s clan, especially the Copts, who continually tormented them. Al-sawm here denotes inflicting torment while keeping its victims alive: Pharaoh’s people repeatedly killed their sons and spared their women in order to enslave them. This deliverance and ordeal were a great test from their Lord, recalled in order to strengthen faith in the Mighty, all-laudable God.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains al-taʾaddhun as a proclamation or declaration. The proclamation that gratitude brings increase and ingratitude a severe punishment is apparently a reminder connected to the command to remember Allah’s blessing: they are to remember both their deliverance and this divine declaration. It may also be linked to their deliverance itself, since the declaration is a blessing in that it encourages good and warns against loss in this world and the Hereafter.

Gratitude means using blessings in a way that remembers the generosity of their giver; it brings an increase of blessing, while ingratitude exposes one to severe consequences. The promise is stated explicitly—“I will surely enhance you (in blessing)”—whereas punishment is alluded to as “My punishment is indeed severe,” rather than directly declaring that every act of ingratitude will be punished. This is the manner of nobility in joining promise to warning.

The verse contains no restriction confining either increase or punishment to this world or the Hereafter. Although it has been cited to establish the obligation of gratitude, its principal emphasis is the danger of disbelief; God’s severity of punishment does not mean that He has explicitly decreed punishment for every instance of disbelief.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan takes Moses’ statement as reinforcing the preceding promise of increase for gratitude and the warning against ingratitude, and as extending through the following ten verses. Even if all people on earth were faithless, Allah would remain all-sufficient: He gains nothing from gratitude and is not harmed by disbelief, while the consequences of human acts return solely to human beings.

Allah is all-laudable because every one of His acts is beautiful and worthy of praise, whether or not anyone recognizes or voices that praise. His grandeur cannot be diminished by silence or disbelief. Indeed, all things praise Him through their very existence: “There is not a thing but celebrates His praise” (al-Isrā’:44).
verses.9:
Al-Mizan regards this as part of Moses’ reminder of God’s past decrees. The “account” or nabaʾ of the earlier peoples concerns their momentous downfall and extinction. Noah, ʿĀd, and Thamūd are examples, while “those who were after them, whom no one knows (well) except Allah” broadens the reference to numerous nations whose particular histories are not comprehensively known. This latter clause is plausibly parenthetical; treating it as a predicate of “those who were after them” is untenable.

The apostles brought manifest proofs that made the truth clear, but their peoples “put their hands in their mouths,” a metaphor indicating that they suppressed and silenced the messengers. Other proposed explanations—gesturing for silence, biting fingers in rage, or treating “hands” as the returned proofs, blessings, or teachings—cannot exhaust the profundity of the divine expression.

Their declaration, “We disbelieve in what you have been sent with,” denies the divine law brought by the apostles, while their grave doubt about what the apostles invite them to expresses doubt about the Unity of Lordship (tawḥīd al-Rubūbīyyah).
verses.10:
Al-Mizan treats “the originator of the heavens and the earth” as more than a reminder that God created the universe. The root of faṭara signifies cleaving, and when attributed to God evokes His bringing beings out of non-existence through providence, as though non-existence were split and existents brought forth from it. “Create,” in the sense of assembling components, does not adequately convey the argument. The idolaters did not deny a maker of the cosmos; their dispute concerned the unity of Lordship and worship. The title “originator” therefore supplies evidence that the One upon whom all existence depends is also the sole Lord.

The messengers answer two doubts raised by the disbelievers: their doubt about divine unity and their rejection of prophethood. The first answer begins from the observable fact that every entity is bounded, distinguished from others, changeable, and unable to sustain its own existence, attributes, or effects. Each therefore depends upon another. God brings every such thing into being, gives it its limits, and distinguishes it, while His own existence is intrinsic and unlimited. Were He limited, He too would require something else to define Him; and what has no boundary cannot be multiplied or divided. He is consequently one and unique.

Because God owns the existence of all things, He manages every aspect of them just as He originates them. No other being possesses independent control over itself or anything else, so none can share His Lordship. This proof establishes not merely an unspecified creator or an isolated act of providence, but God’s existence as the foundation of every being and effect, from which His unity in Lordship follows. It is accessible even to an ordinary mind because it begins with the reality of the world rather than treating existence as an illusion.

The words “He calls you” answer the denial of prophethood. Divine care guides every kind of being toward its proper perfection and happiness, and human beings are no exception. Human life continues beyond death: worldly happiness lies in an upright and balanced life, while happiness in the hereafter rests on true belief and good action. Although human nature contains an innate summons toward right belief and conduct, social life also excites desire, injustice, and deviation. If natural inclination alone were sufficient, societies and individuals would not become corrupt. Providence therefore requires an additional means of guidance: prophethood, a human station that receives true beliefs and righteous laws through revelation and unseen communication and conveys them to others.

Following that call serves both worlds. In earthly life, a community’s sins and injustices expose it to destructive punishment; uprightness allows it to live out its appointed course without such sudden retribution. For the hereafter, faith and God-conscious action refine the soul and remove the stains of sin in proportion to one’s obedience. Thus “that He may forgive some of your sins” states the otherworldly end of the prophetic call, while respite until a specified term states its worldly end. The hereafter is mentioned first because it is the primary and lasting abode. The messengers attribute the invitation to God, correcting the disbelievers’ attempt to portray it as merely the messengers’ own project.

The specification “some of your sins” is meaningful rather than redundant. It may indicate forgiveness proportionate to obedience and the fact that a human community never becomes wholly free of sins carrying consequences. Al-Mizan rejects confining it simply to God’s rights rather than people’s rights, since reports state that Islam effaces what preceded it. It also finds weak the proposals that “some” really means all sins indiscriminately, only pre-conversion sins, or only major sins. The different Qur’anic wording used for believers and disbelievers may honour the station of faith by explicitly promising believers forgiveness of all sins while promising disbelievers some and remaining silent about the rest; the limited wording does not itself deny further forgiveness.

The specified term is an immutable deadline at which punishment can no longer be deferred, distinct from a suspended term that may change. The disbelievers nevertheless answer that the messengers are only humans like themselves, accuse them of wanting to sever inherited worship, and demand manifest authority. Their humanity is made the basis of rejection: if they possess no perceptible distinction, the claim to an unseen connection appears to the disbelievers like a worldly attempt to displace ancestral custom. Since revelation and prophethood transcend ordinary experience, a claimant must authenticate that exceptional connection by another event beyond the ordinary course—a miraculous sign. Their demand therefore asks for a clear proof that compels recognition of the claimed prophetic relation to the unseen.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan explains that the messengers accept that they are human beings like their opponents, but deny that shared humanity precludes revelation and prophethood. Just as intellectual and bodily perfections occur in some human beings rather than others, Allah may favor whichever of His servants He wills with this special gift.

The demand for a manifest authority rests on the mistaken assumption that a prophet has a celestial nature or independent unseen power by which he can produce whatever sign he wishes. A messenger is a human recipient of revelation, not an autonomous controller of affairs; he may bring a sign only by Allah’s leave. Thus, the messengers do not deny the possibility of producing the requested miraculous sign, but deny any independent power to do so.

Their command that the faithful trust in Allah supplies a further argument: all power, strength, origination, sustenance, and return belong to Him, and no being holds authority except by His permission. Therefore believers must entrust every affair to their Lord, and a messenger must recognize that even a miraculous sign comes only through divine permission.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan explains the question, “And why should we not put our trust in Allah?” as a rhetorical negation: there is no excuse for the messengers not to rely on Him. Allah has guided them in their ways—that is, in the religious laws they proclaim—without any contribution from them to this blessing and happiness. His guidance is therefore proof that reliance upon Him is obligatory: He does not betray His servants and intends their good.

Their resolve to bear whatever torment their opponents inflict follows from this reliance. Guided believers will patiently endure harm in calling to Allah, awaiting His decree rather than resorting to any apparent power or strength of their own.

The statement, “in Allah let all the trusting put their trust,” gives Allah exclusive priority as the proper object of trust. Although anyone who truly trusts should place that trust in Him, genuine reliance belongs only to the believer, who recognizes that all affairs belong to Allah and consequently obeys His commands, avoids His prohibitions, accepts His decrees, and dislikes what He dislikes. This is the reality of faith.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan explains that, having failed in argument against the messengers, the faithless threatened both them and their followers with expulsion unless they entered the unbelievers’ creed. The threat particularly included believers who had formerly belonged to that creed. “Or you shall revert to our creed” denotes a transition into their religion and does not imply that the messengers themselves had previously followed it; the emphatic wording conveys an ultimatum to expel them or compel this return.

Allah then revealed to the messengers that He would destroy the wrongdoers and settle them in the land after them. Calling the opponents “wrongdoers” indicates the reason for their destruction. The promise is conditional upon fearing Allah’s maqām—His authority and comprehensive oversight, or His station—and fearing His waʿīd, the punishments with which He warns those who disobey. Both forms of fear amount to piety (taqwa).

The Lord of the messengers, whose special lordship toward them accompanies their reliance and brings mercy and care, thus promises to destroy those who threaten them, grant the messengers inheritance of the land from which they were threatened with expulsion, and give it to His pious servants.

verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains istaftaḥū as seeking victory and divine support, and khaybah as hopeless disappointment, defeat, and destruction. The pronoun in “they prayed for victory” apparently refers to the messengers, who sought Allah’s help when every means had failed and oppression and denial had reached their height. It may also include both messengers and disbelievers, since the latter repeatedly demanded the decisive fulfillment of the promised judgment. On either reading, every obstinate, defiant tyrant was disappointed and subjected to severe punishment.

Hell lies before such a tyrant. Its drink is ṣadīd, the pus that flows from a wound. He repeatedly gulps it, yet can scarcely force it down his throat; death comes at him from every direction, but he does not die, and a further harsh punishment awaits him.

verses.18: Al-Mizan explains the “tempestuous day” as a metaphor for the consequences of unbelievers’ deeds: like ash violently scattered by wind until nothing remains, those deeds achieve neither happiness nor salvation. The image is complete as stated, requiring neither extrapolation nor a supplied introductory formula. It appears that the verse is not part of Prophet Moses’s speech, but the conclusion drawn from the message just conveyed.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that ruʾyah here means decisive knowledge, not sight. To create the heavens and earth bi al-ḥaqq is to create them in inseparable association with truth: every divine act has a purpose and moves toward an end. An aimless act is bāṭil, and an ordered but purposeless act is play; hence the enduring, interconnected order of creation cannot be a game. The bā in bi al-ḥaqq therefore denotes accompaniment, not the means of creation or merely its intended purpose.

Creation in truth also discloses God’s omnipotence and self-sufficiency. Were the world play, it would imply a need in God, such as diversion or relief, which His self-sufficiency excludes. The address, though made through the Prophet, concerns humanity generally: God can remove them and bring a new creation, and this is effortless precisely because He is Allah.

Al-Mizan holds that mentioning a new creation is necessary. Removing humanity while leaving the present, mutually dependent cosmos unchanged would render that order purposeless; likewise, annihilating creation without a further end would be futile. Divine truth and self-sufficiency are instead shown in replacing one people with another.

verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains barazū as emerging into open manifestation: on the Day of Judgment people will find themselves before God with no veil between themselves and Him. This is from their perspective, since they had imagined themselves hidden from, or absent from, their Lord in the world; nothing is ever hidden from God. The phrase may also signify that they are called to account and that their promised requital is carried out.

The weak are the disbelievers who followed influential disbelieving leaders, while the arrogant are those leaders who turned people from faith and denied God’s signs. The followers ask whether their former leaders can repel any of God’s punishment. The leaders answer that, had God guided them, they would have guided their followers; this may mean guidance away from punishment or guidance to true faith in the world. In either case, despair and patience are now equal, for there is no escape from the inevitable punishment.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan identifies the Satan speaking on the Day of Judgment as Iblīs, the principal source of temptation and misguidance for Adam’s children, though his progeny may influence particular persons or acts. His speech publicly unveils the real nature of his worldly relationship with the wrongdoers, when all false objects of devotion, leaders, and companions disavow those who associated them with God.

Iblīs contrasts God’s true promise with his own false and broken promise. God’s promise includes the consequences of faith and polytheism in this life, as well as resurrection, judgment, Paradise, and hellfire. Iblīs, by contrast, enticed people with desires, long hopes, fear of poverty, humiliation, and others’ blame. He made them forget death and the Hereafter, obscured their Lord’s position, and induced them to treat immediate causes and their own souls as independent controllers, so that they relied on themselves rather than God. His promises either pursued what cannot be attained or made attained things appear other than expected.

His claim that he had no sulṭān over them denies both coercive dominion over their persons and possessions and any compelling proof that could force their minds to accept polytheism. Al-Mizan takes “except that I called you” as a discontinuous exception: he merely called them, without authority, and they answered. Calling does not itself give the caller control over the called. It therefore rejects al-Rāzī’s view that Satan’s whispering constitutes the authority excepted in the verse; any inclination created by answering him is a power the followers impose upon themselves, not a power inherent in Satan over them. Satan’s authority is conditional upon people’s following and befriending him and associating partners with God, not the cause of that following.

Thus Iblīs tells them to blame themselves, because they control their acts and bear their consequences. This does not establish that their control is absolute. Neither side can answer the other’s cry for help or intercede for the other: their supposed bond is severed and their following has profited neither side. His disavowal concerns their having made him a partner through obedience, rather than through worship alone. Their former association was an illusion, and the wrongdoers’ painful punishment returns to their own wrongdoing.
verses.23: Al-Mizan says that the verse describes the final state of believers who have faith and perform righteous deeds: they are admitted by their Lord’s leave into everlasting gardens with flowing streams. Their mutual greeting is peace, in contrast to the disputes, mutual disavowal, and despair of the preceding wrongdoers.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan takes the construction as likening a good word to a good tree. Its stable root is deeply fixed in the earth, its branches extend upward, and it continually yields beneficial fruit by its Lord’s permission. Competing identifications of the word, the tree, and “every season” distract from the verse’s purpose.

The good word is a firm, true belief expressed as an utterance grounded in settled conviction and steadfast action, not a bare phrase. In its primary contextual sense it is the word of monotheism and the testimony that there is no deity but God, truly realized and maintained. This accords with the following statement that God fortifies believers with a firm word in this world and the Hereafter.

Monotheism has a root protected from alteration, decay, and falsehood—either the exalted divine name or the realities themselves. From it grow subsidiary true beliefs, pure character, and righteous deeds, by which believers live wholesomely and rightly build the human world in harmony with the universal order. Those who say, “Our Lord is Allah,” and remain steadfast most fully resemble this rooted, fruitful tree, from whose existence people continually benefit. The parable applies generally to every true word and righteous deed, but emphasizes monotheism as the foundation from which the rest arise. It admonishes that happiness and salvation require realizing this word and remaining steadfast upon it.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan takes the construction as likening a good word to a good tree. Its stable root is deeply fixed in the earth, its branches extend upward, and it continually yields beneficial fruit by its Lord’s permission. Competing identifications of the word, the tree, and “every season” distract from the verse’s purpose.

verses.26: Al-Mizan explains the bad word as the opposite of the good word: it is the word of polytheism, represented by a corrupt tree uprooted from the earth. Having no firm root or stability, it produces only harm and evil. Debates over particular plants do not alter this meaning.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan links “with a firm word” to God’s act of fortifying, and likewise takes “in the life of this world and in the Hereafter” as describing that divine fortification. When believers adhere to faith and uprightness, God strengthens their chosen steadfastness in both realms; without His strengthening, their steadfastness would yield them no benefit.

Guidance begins with God. He created people with an innate disposition to know His lordship, inspired them with immorality and piety, and reinforced this original guidance through the prophetic call. Whoever adheres to this disposition and seeks knowledge and good deeds is guided further by God. Misguidance, however, begins with a person’s own deviation, ignorance of God’s station, immersion in worldly concerns, and following of desire; God then recompenses that choice with further misguidance. Thus the believer’s sound choice is fortified against deviation, while the wrongdoers—here disbelievers in God and His signs—are deprived of guidance.

The verse concludes the parable of the rooted good tree and the unstable bad tree. The faithful are like the firmly rooted tree that grows and bears fruit; the disbelievers attain neither a sound worldly life nor abiding blessing and divine pleasure in the Hereafter, but meet doubt, indecision, anxiety, sorrow, regret, and remorse. God guides some and leads others astray as He wills, with no impediment to His act; He is the doer of both, in accordance with the destined happiness of the believer and misery of the disbeliever.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse concerns, generally, the leaders of disbelief and misguidance among former nations and this Ummah, not specifically the Meccan disbelievers or those killed at Badr. They are singled out because their influence causes communities to obey them. Surrounded by God’s grace, including creation and the enduring effects of the word of truth, they replace the gratitude due for that grace—or the grace itself—with disbelief.

By leading their people into the abode of ruin, these chiefs also lead themselves there: they go astray and make others go astray. The abode of ruin is hell, an evil dwelling, and their leading people to it means sealing them in its misery even before death or entry into it. The following warning is read as continuing to address these disbelievers and as emphasizing their final misery. Al-Mizan therefore rejects a reading that restricts the passage to a particular Meccan event.

verses.30:
Al-Mizan explains al-andād as equals or counterparts: beings such as angels, jinn, and humans whom the polytheists set beside God. Though they admitted these beings were created by God, they called them gods and lords, ascribed worldly governance to them, and worshipped them from fear and hope, despite creation and command belonging only to God.

Their natural disposition and the proofs brought by prophets already attested God’s oneness; they were not simply ignorant or mistaken about Tawḥīd. Rather, they deliberately made such equals in pursuit of worldly advantage, to dominate people, and to lead them from God’s way. The command to tell them to enjoy themselves briefly exposes this concealed motive while warning that their destination is hellfire.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains that, after warning those who mislead people, God commands His believing servants to follow His path before the Day of Judgment. On that day, material exchange and worldly friendship cannot recover lost happiness, because it is the day of reckoning and requital.

Maintaining prayer and spending from God’s provision summarize the religious duties that set human life right in relation both to God and to other people. The infāq is general spending in God’s way, not the later prescribed zakāt, and it should be given secretly or openly as religious propriety requires.

The negation of friendship does not contradict the survival and benefit of friendship founded on piety: all other friendship ends. Similarly, intercession is negated in one respect yet affirmed where God permits it.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as proof of God’s exclusive lordship against those who set up equals to Him. He created the heavens and earth, sends down rain that sustains plant and animal life, makes ships useful for human transport and goods, provides flowing rivers, and subjects the sun, moon, night, and day to humanity. The subjection of ships means their being made useful, not merely that people were inspired to build and use them; their sailing, though occurring through natural causes, remains by God’s all-encompassing command. The sun and moon are dā’ibīn, continuously and enduringly following their courses.

“Asking” is the demand produced by need in rational beings, whether conveyed by speech, gesture, or writing. In its true sense every needy being asks God alone, even when someone verbally asks another, because God is the ultimate source to whom all needs turn. His unrestricted “giving” means that every human need is met through His generosity, in full in some cases and in part in others, even though an individual may find a particular request unfulfilled. Sincere prayer made by the supplicant himself is not rejected; apparent non-response may arise from insincerity, a disjunction between heart and tongue, mistaken wording, or a prayer that is not truly one’s own.

The min in “from all that you had asked Him” is initiatory: what He gives proceeds from the whole range of what is asked, sometimes comprising all and sometimes part of a request. It is not distributive, as though every request necessarily received only a portion, nor does the wording claim that every request is wholly granted.

God’s blessings cannot be numerically enumerated. The universe’s parts, attributes, and states are mutually interconnected, each benefiting others, so everything is a blessing in relation to the whole. The singular “blessing of Allah” itself conveys this abundance. Humanity’s frequent failure to recognize and thank these gifts is injustice to itself, or injustice toward the blessings themselves, and leads to ruin and loss.

verses.35:
Al-Mizan holds that Abraham’s prayer to make Mecca a sanctuary is apparently distinct from his prayer in al-Baqarah to make it a secure town and provide its believing people with fruits. The differing wording and objects of the two prayers suggest different occasions: on one return Abraham found Jurhum near Ishmael and his mother and prayed that the place become a town and that its believers receive fruits; on a later return, after it had become a town, he prayed that it be made secure. The present prayer was therefore, apparently, Abraham’s last Qur’anic prayer: after the Sacred House had been built and Mecca inhabited. If the two reports are instead taken as one prayer, the differing expressions can be explained by ellipsis.

The security Abraham sought was legislative, not natural: he asked God to decree Mecca sacred and safe. This decree, established through Abraham by God’s permission, is among God’s greatest blessings, for reverence for the Ancient House and its sanctuary has endured in people’s hearts and brought religious and worldly benefit to inhabitants and those attached to it.

By wajnubnī, Abraham asks God to keep him and his descendants from worshipping idols because idols have led many astray. The idols’ being described as misleading signifies their intrinsic causal connection with misguidance, not necessarily a conscious action. Preservation from idolatry is a divine mercy and empowerment, yet it neither coerces the servant nor removes free choice. Good acts and abstention from evil are first attributed to God and then to the servant, whereas evil is first attributed to the servant; even when it is attributed to God, this is only by way of requital. The servant possesses guidance and avoidance only through God’s enabling, while God possesses them inherently. Thus Abraham asks for the servants’ own abstention from idolatry, guidance when they are receptive to truth, and divine blessing when they seek it. Although the wording is general, its benefit reaches those receptive to it, not the obstinate and arrogant.

“His children” can naturally include all later descendants, both the progeny of Ishmael and of Isaac, though the context may be taken as more particularly concerned with Ishmael’s family in Hijaz. “My Lord! Indeed, they have led astray many among the people” gives the reason for the request and repeats the appeal to divine mercy.

Al-Mizan explains “So whoever follows me indeed belongs to me” as following Abraham’s path, not merely affirming divine unity. It means accepting his religion and law in belief and practice, walking the monotheistic path, seeking God’s mercy, and avoiding idols. Conversely, disobeying Abraham means abandoning that path, wholly or partly, in belief or practice. His followers, whether or not biologically descended from him, are associated with him and included in his request for protection; those who do not follow him, even if physically descended from him, are not counted as belonging to him. Biological descent alone therefore does not settle inclusion in, or exclusion from, a lineage.

Abraham does not explicitly ask forgiveness for those who disobey him, but leaves them to God’s forgiveness and mercy. This may implicitly present to divine grace those who have departed from his path, since such disobedience does not itself exclude mercy. It cannot mean polytheism itself, however, because associating partners with God is not forgiven; the intended disobedience is other than shirk.

The commentary rejects attempts to treat the prayer for Abraham and his descendants as an unanswered prayer. Some limit “descendants” to Ishmael and Isaac, or to monotheists then living; others say the prayer was accepted for some descendants only. The first two conflict with the apparent wording, while the third misses the issue that the Qur’an would not recount an irrelevant, uncorrected prayer in this manner. Claims that Abraham’s polytheist descendants did not literally worship idols—because they merely treated them as intermediaries, worshipped other sorts of objects, or performed stone-circumambulation rather than idol worship—do not solve the matter, since the essential error is association in worship.

Nor does Al-Mizan accept that Abraham, though infallible, asked merely for continued steadfastness, spoke only in humility, or sought protection only from hidden shirk. To separate a bestowed divine protection from its Giver would wrongly make its recipient self-sufficient: the servant remains dependent after receiving grace, and God’s sovereignty and power remain unchanged. Supplication expresses need, not a supposed lack in God’s decree. Humility cannot sensibly negate or cast doubt on a foundational certainty such as prophetic infallibility. Hidden shirk concerns reliance upon and orientation toward other than God, whereas Abraham’s stated reason concerns the misleading of idols and his request concerns explicit idol worship; extending “idols” and “worship” to every such orientation has no supporting evidence.

The commentary likewise rejects explanations that make Abraham’s words about disobedient people a plea for forgiveness of persistent polytheists. There is no evidence that earlier laws forgave polytheism; Qur’anic evidence instead indicates that polytheists cannot attain salvation through intercession or any means except repentance before death. Reading forgiveness as conditional on repentance arbitrarily restricts the wording and disrupts the contrast between followers and disobedient people, since one who repents becomes a follower. Explaining forgiveness as conversion from polytheism, or mercy as merely concealing the sin in this world and delaying punishment, conflicts with the apparent sense of pardoning sin and removing its consequences. It is especially implausible that Abraham, God’s friend in his later life, was ignorant that polytheism is unforgivable, and the suggestion that “disobedience” simply means non-polytheistic sins requires the very contextual explanation already supplied. Thus the proposed difficulties arise from missing the verse’s distinction between Abraham’s true followers and those who depart from his path, and from confusing ordinary disobedience with shirk.

verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains that “part of my descendants” denotes a portion of Abraham’s progeny: Ishmael and those born from his line, not Ishmael alone, as shown by the plural purpose, “so that they may give thanks.” “A barren valley” (ghayr dhī zarʿin) means a land without vegetation and unsuitable for cultivation. The House is attributed to God because it was built exclusively for His worship, and its being muḥarram means that God legislatively made it sacred; “by Your sacred House” qualifies Abraham’s settling of his descendants.

The wording supports the view that this prayer came late in Abraham’s life, after he had built the Kaʿbah and Mecca had been constructed and inhabited, rather than on the day he first brought Ishmael and his mother to an empty, barren land. On this view there is no need for conjectures that Abraham was informed beforehand that he would build the House there, or that the House had existed and been destroyed or raised to heaven.

Abraham settled them in a valley lacking worldly comforts and inhabitants so that they might devote themselves wholly to worship and maintain prayer without worldly distraction. His request that some people’s hearts incline toward them means that people should be drawn to them, either by dwelling among them or making the Hajj to the Sacred House. The request for fruits indicates that trade should be directed toward them, so that they may give thanks.
verses.38: Al-Mizan says that the verse is clear in affirming that God knows all that people conceal and disclose. “Nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heavens” may either continue Abraham’s speech—explaining that God knows because nothing escapes Him—or be God’s own statement. On the former reading, “the heavens” may signify what is hidden from human sensory perception, while “the earth” signifies what is manifest to it.
verses.39: Al-Mizan regards Abraham’s praise as an interjection within his supplications, recalling God’s immense favor in granting him the righteous sons Ishmael and Isaac despite his old age, when ordinary means of having children had failed. Since they were granted in answer to his fervent request for offspring, he praises and thanks God both for the gift and for answering his prayer.
verses.40: Al-Mizan reads Abraham’s request to be made a maintainer of prayer as reliance on God, like his plea for protection from idol worship: establishing prayer belongs to God in permission and will, and to the servant in commitment and action. This second supplication, shared by Abraham and his descendants, follows their plea for protection from idols and precedes the joint plea for forgiveness of Abraham, his parents, and all the faithful. Abraham singles himself out because his request also embraces his descendants’ rights, while “my children” and “my descendants” mean only some of them. “Our Lord, accept my supplication” adds insistence and emphasis, paralleling his earlier reason that idols led many astray.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan identifies this as the final part of Abraham’s Qur’anic supplication: he closes by asking forgiveness for himself, his parents, and all believers on the Day of Reckoning, in a manner resembling Noah’s closing prayer for himself, his parents, and believing men and women.

The verse supports the conclusion that Abraham was not the son of Āzar, the idolater. In his old age Abraham prays for his parents, whereas he had already repudiated Āzar after fulfilling his earlier promise to seek forgiveness for him, once Āzar’s enmity to God became manifest.

The commentary also notes Abraham’s precise alternation between “My Lord” and “Our Lord”: he uses the former for matters particular to himself, such as his foremostness and the station of Imām, and the latter for matters shared with others.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains that God is not unaware or neglectful of the wrongdoers, despite their prosperity, arrogance, and corruption on earth. He merely grants them respite until the Day of Resurrection.

Shakhaṣa baṣaruhu denotes eyes whose eyelids no longer move or blink, while muhṭiʿ describes one raising and extending his neck and head. Thus, on that day their gaze will be fixed and unblinking, their heads upturned, and their hearts empty of understanding, reflection, and planning—either through the extremity of their obstinacy or because terror has deprived them of their senses. The verse warns the wrongdoers and consoles others.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains that God is not unaware or neglectful of the wrongdoers, despite their prosperity, arrogance, and corruption on earth. He merely grants them respite until the Day of Resurrection.

Shakhaṣa baṣaruhu denotes eyes whose eyelids no longer move or blink, while muhṭiʿ describes one raising and extending his neck and head. Thus, on that day their gaze will be fixed and unblinking, their heads upturned, and their hearts empty of understanding, reflection, and planning—either through the extremity of their obstinacy or because terror has deprived them of their senses. verses.44:
Al-Mizan distinguishes this warning from the preceding warning. The earlier verses concern the inescapable punishment of the Day of Resurrection, from which neither a sinful nation nor any individual wrongdoer can escape. The present warning concerns worldly eradication: a punishment that inevitably overtakes a transgressing nation, though some individuals among it may be spared. It is therefore neither the Day of Resurrection nor the day of death. Believers are not included in this eradication; rather, it seizes the wrongdoers among a nation.

This is a fixed divine course in the encounter between nations and their messengers, including the Ummah of the Prophet Muḥammad. It culminates in the cleansing of the earth from polytheism and oppression, leaving believers so that worship belongs wholly to God and His righteous servants inherit the earth. The objection that the preceding statement—God grants respite until the day when eyes are glazed—restricts all punishment to the Resurrection is answered by distinguishing the unavoidable otherworldly punishment from the additional worldly punishment. Restricting this verse itself to the Resurrection would depart from its evident context and conflict with verses concerning the coming punishment of this community.

The wrongdoers are those among the people whom this established punishment does not pass over. Their plea for a short respite asks for a brief return to worldly life to repair what their injustice caused them to miss, as shown by their wish to answer God’s call and follow the messengers. The plural “messengers,” although the passage concerns this community, shows that the issue is the truth of the messenger’s call and rejection of it, rather than the person of one particular messenger.

Their former oath that there would be no reverse is a decisive, emphatic assertion: before punishment came, they regarded themselves, because of their strength, domination, and defenses, as an imperishable nation controlling events. They are reproached for seeking respite after having made that claim. The reproach is reinforced by their having inhabited the dwellings of earlier self-wronging peoples: they had both observed what befell those peoples and received illustrative warnings that denial of truth and rejection of the prophetic call bring an overwhelming punishment.

verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains that God encompasses the wrongdoers’ plots in knowledge and power. A plot succeeds only against one unaware of it; when its target knows of it and can repel it—especially when it is returned upon its plotters—it loses its effect. Thus God knows and can counter their scheme even if it were powerful enough to move mountains.

A possible interpretation takes in as negative and “mountains” as an allegory for divine signs and miracles: their plots cannot nullify God’s signs. This is associated with Ibn Masʿūd’s recitation, wa mā kāna makruhum, but Al-Mizan deems it remote. Another recitation of li-tazūl gives the established sense that their plots were so formidable as to make mountains crumble.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan takes the verse as the consequence of the preceding discussion: punishment may be deferred until the Day of Resurrection, but God will not break His promise to support His messengers and punish those who oppose their call. A promise is broken either through inability to fulfill it or a change imposed by circumstances; neither applies to God, whose absolute might leaves Him neither impotent nor subject to an external force.

As the Avenger, God exacts retribution for the truth against those who arrogantly defy it and for the oppressed against their oppressors. This name is consistently joined in the Qur’an with His might, for His vengeance follows from His being al-ʿAzīz.

Al-Mizan distinguishes personal revenge, which arises from an injured person’s emotional desire for satisfaction, from rational and social retribution. The latter protects social order, preserves rights, and enforces just laws; punishment is then a legal and social right arising from the offender’s evil. Divine revenge belongs to this latter kind: it vindicates the rights of divine religion and heavenly law, and at times the rights of oppressed individuals. God is exalted above being emotionally injured by sin or benefited by obedience.

The objection that divine revenge is meaningless if God has no personal need for it, and that mercy should rule out eternal punishment, confuses personal with rational retribution and emotional with rational mercy. Rational mercy seeks to reform one capable of reform; eternal punishment applies only where reform is no longer possible, when a person is besieged by his iniquity. From another perspective, beyond the language of reward and punishment, the evil forms of deeds manifest after death in the soul through the bad dispositions acquired during worldly life.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan explains that the transformation of earth and heavens and humanity’s presentation before God describe the Day of Rising, the supreme manifestation of divine retribution, though God’s retribution is not confined to that day. “The earth” is the earth now inhabited, and “the heavens” are these heavens; both will be altered from their present state.

Reports and interpretations variously portray the earth as silver, fire, bread, or a differently transformed place for different groups, while another view describes its leveling and the removal of its mountains, vegetation, sun, moon, and stars. Their divergence, even if the reports were sound, indicates that these outward depictions are illustrative examples rather than the intended literal meaning. The Qur’anic descriptions of the earth glowing with its Lord’s light and mountains moving like a mirage show that this transformation exceeds familiar physical changes: the system and purpose governing earth and heaven on that day will differ from the worldly system.

To be presented before Allah, the One, the All-paramount, is to appear before Him after the worldly barriers that obscure this reality have vanished. Although nothing is ever hidden from God, they will then find Him witnessing, dominating, and encompassing every direction and condition, with no power exercising any influence over them besides Him. Their unimpeded standing before Him follows from His oneness, on which all existence depends, and His overpowering supremacy.

The guilty will be joined together in shackles, clothed in garments of pitch, and covered in the face by Fire. Every soul will receive precisely what it has earned, good or evil. This recompense is not punishment for a personal vendetta, but the manifestation and exact return of what deeds have procured. God’s swiftness in reckoning means that no delay intervenes in this requital; alternatively, the judgment and recording occur with the deed while its manifestation comes on the Day of Resurrection. In reality, the two explanations coincide.

verses.52:
Al-Mizan holds that this concluding proclamation refers most fittingly to the clarifications of this particular chapter, not to the whole Qur’an or only to the passage beginning, “Do not suppose that Allah is oblivious of what the wrongdoers are doing.” Its stated purposes—warning, knowledge that God is One, and admonition for those endowed with intellect—are what human understanding can grasp of a matter whose fuller divine reality exceeds it.

It warns of the imminent and unavoidable retribution of transgressors, supplies clear proofs of monotheism, and reminds believers of the divine knowledge it contains. The conclusion corresponds to the chapter’s opening, where the Book was sent so that mankind might be brought from darkness into light by their Lord’s command and to the path of the All-mighty, the All-laudable. Those who answer the call and believe pass from the darkness of unbelief to the light of faith; those who resist are still warned and brought from ignorance to knowledge of divine oneness, though this entails danger and loss. Thus all are warned and informed of God’s oneness, while the admonition is especially for those possessing discernment.
